title.en: Possessives: мой, твой, наш, ваш, свой, его́

card: **мой, твой, наш, ваш, свой** agree with the thing owned, like adjectives: **моя́ кни́га**, **в моём до́ме**. **его́** (*his*), **её** (*her*), **их** (*their*) **never change**. **свой** means *one's own*, referring back to the subject: **Он лю́бит свою́ жену́** (his own wife).

sections.body:
Russian possessives behave like adjectives: they agree with the **owned** thing, not with the owner. So a woman says **мой брат** and a man says **моя́ сестра́**: the ending is about the brother or the sister, not about the speaker.

The third person is different: **его́, её, их** are frozen genitive forms of **он, она́, они́** (*of him, of her, of them*), so they never change.

sections.title: свой: the reflexive possessive
sections.body:
When the owner is the **subject of the same clause**, Russian prefers **свой**: **Я чита́ю свою́ кни́гу** = **Я чита́ю мою́ кни́гу** (both fine for *I*/*you*), but with *he, she, they* the choice changes the meaning:

- **Он лю́бит свою́ жену́.** *He loves his (own) wife.*
- **Он лю́бит его́ жену́.** *He loves his (another man's) wife!*

So with a third-person subject, **свой** points back to the subject and **его́/её/их** point to someone else. **свой** is never used in the subject itself: *His wife is here* is **Его́ жена́ здесь.**

English *his* can be ambiguous: *Tom took his car* (his own? someone else's?). Russian forces a decision: **свою́ маши́ну** or **его́ маши́ну**. English also uses possessives where Russian leaves them out: *I washed my hands* is simply **Я помы́л ру́ки**.

mistakes.why: Her own bag, and she is the subject: **свою́**. **её** would mean another woman's bag.
**его́, её, их** never change, whatever the case of the noun.

examples.en: Their children are already grown up.
